description: Antigone buries her brother against the order of King Creon. Sophocles sets up a conflict that has never gone away: the law of the state, or a higher moral duty?

hero.hook: A king forbids the burial of a traitor. A sister disobeys. Two kinds of justice collide, and Thebes falls apart.

blocks.text: **Antigone** is the daughter of Oedipus and Jocasta. Around **441 BC**, the playwright **Sophocles** made her the heroine of a play that became universal.

Facing King **Creon**, she asks a question that crosses the centuries: when a law of the state contradicts a higher moral conviction, do you obey or resist? This is not good against evil. It is two ideas of justice crashing into each other.

In [[Thebes]], after the exile of Oedipus, his sons **Eteocles** and **Polynices** were supposed to rule in turn. Eteocles refuses to hand over power. Polynices attacks his own city with a foreign army. The two brothers kill each other.

blocks.caption: Antigone before Creon: family piety against the order of the state

blocks.text: Creon, their uncle, takes power. Eteocles, defender of the city, will get a solemn funeral. Polynices, treated as a traitor, will get no grave at all. For the Greeks this is terrifying: with no rites, the soul wanders by the [[Styx]], the river of the underworld, and never rests.
A single handful of earth was enough, symbolically, to perform the burial rite. Antigone's act is quiet, and its consequences are enormous.

sections.title: Two dead brothers, one cruel decree

blocks.text: Antigone refuses. She does not deny that Polynices betrayed the city. She argues that no king can cancel what is owed to the dead. Her sister **Ismene** hesitates, careful. Antigone acts alone and covers the body.

blocks.caption: Antigone performing the burial rite for Polynices

blocks.text: In front of Creon, she claims [[Natural law]]: rules that are “unwritten and unshakeable,” older than any human decree. Creon sees a threat to the state. He sentences her to be walled up alive.

**Haemon**, son of Creon and betrothed to Antigone, tries to reason with his father. Creon shuts himself off. The seer **Tiresias** announces the anger of the gods: the city is polluted by the abandoned corpse and by the imprisonment of Antigone.

blocks.caption: At the tomb, too late: the tragedy carries off Antigone and Haemon

blocks.text: Creon gives in at last, too late. Antigone has hanged herself. Haemon kills himself. **Eurydice**, Creon's wife, takes her own life. Trying to save the law, Creon has destroyed his family. He is left alone, king of an order that means nothing.

Sophocles does not make Creon a simple villain. He is a leader who wants to keep chaos out. Antigone, for her part, is utterly rigid. The [[Hegelian dialectic of Antigone]] reads the play as a collision of two spheres: the family against the city.
In 1944, [[Jean Anouilh's Antigone]] was staged under the Occupation. German censors saw Creon's order in it. French audiences often read it as the heroism of the Resistance.

The clash between individual conscience and reasons of state is still at the center of political thought. Antigone is a reminder that absolute justice, with no dialogue, can destroy the very people it claims to defend.
Antigone sets the sacred laws of the family against Creon's decree. Their shared refusal to compromise ruins Thebes and the royal line.
